The golden calf represents one of the most powerful biblical symbols of spiritual backsliding and misplaced faith. The story appears in Exodus 32. While Moses was on Mount Sinai receiving God's law from God directly, the impatient Israelites demanded that Aaron create a god they could see and worship instead. Aaron collected gold from the people and fashioned it into a calf, a symbol of strength and fertility in the pagan cultures surrounding them. The people then celebrated the golden calf as the god who had brought them out of Egypt, completely abandoning the invisible God of the covenant. When Moses descended from the mountain and discovered this idol worship taking place, he was filled with fury at their rebellion. He smashed the stone tablets of the law and destroyed the idol. The golden calf ultimately became the archetype of idolatry and false worship in Western religious thought. In modern usage, worshipping the golden calf means pursuing wealth, material gain, or shallow pleasures instead of meaningful values or spirituality. The story connects to Moses, who discovered the people's rebellion and destroyed the calf, to Aaron, his brother who made the calf at the people's insistence, and to the book of Exodus which recounts this act of rebellion and idolatry.
